layers.basics: Volts, amps, ohms, farads and henries are units; prefixes like milli- and mega- scale them. Checking units catches many mistakes.
layers.deeper: Dimensional analysis shows that RC has units of seconds and that √(L/C) has units of ohms.
layers.expert: SI base units include the ampere (defined via the elementary charge e=1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ C since 2019); decibels express ratios logarithmically: dB=20log₁₀(V₂/V₁).

title: Kinematics and forces
summary: Describing motion and what causes it.

layers.basics: Position, velocity and acceleration describe motion; Newton’s laws link acceleration to force.
layers.deeper: Mechanical systems (motors, MEMS springs, loudspeaker cones) are modelled with the same equations as circuits.
layers.expert: F=ma; the mass–spring–damper mẍ+bẋ+kx=F is the mechanical twin of series RLC (m↔L, b↔R, k↔1/C).

layers.basics: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only moved; power is energy per time; momentum is conserved in collisions.
layers.deeper: Electric power P=VI is the same idea as mechanical power P=Fv, and electromagnetic fields carry energy and momentum too.
layers.expert: Work–energy theorem W=ΔKE; potential energy of conservative forces; ∮ Poynting vector gives field energy flow.

layers.basics: Torque twists things the way force pushes them; moment of inertia is rotational mass.
layers.deeper: Electric motors and generators convert between electrical power and torque×speed.
layers.expert: τ=Iα; rotational power P=τω; angular momentum L=Iω conserved without external torque; gyroscopic effects underlie MEMS gyros.

title: Charge and Coulomb’s law
summary: Charges push or pull with an inverse-square force.

layers.basics: Like charges repel, unlike attract, and the force falls with the square of distance.
layers.deeper: Charge is conserved and quantised in units of e. Electric field is force per unit charge.
layers.expert: F=kq₁q₂/r², k=1/(4πε₀)≈8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C². Superposition holds, which is why fields of many charges add as vectors.

title: Gauss’s law
summary: Electric flux out of a closed surface counts the enclosed charge.

layers.basics: Surround any region with an imaginary surface: the total electric field passing out is proportional to the charge inside.
layers.deeper: For symmetric charge shapes it gives fields instantly, and shows why the field inside a conductor is zero.

title: Electric potential and voltage
summary: Energy per charge: what we call voltage.

layers.basics: Voltage is the energy a unit charge gains moving between two points; a battery maintains a voltage.
layers.deeper: Potential is a scalar map of the field; equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines. Ground is a chosen zero.
layers.expert: V=−∫E·dl; point charge V=q/4πε₀r; Poisson ∇²V=−ρ/ε₀. In circuits voltage differences are path independent as long as flux is static.

title: Capacitance and dielectrics
summary: Storing charge in an electric field.

layers.basics: Two conductors separated by an insulator store charge when a voltage is applied; the ratio is capacitance.
layers.deeper: A dielectric between the plates increases capacitance by εr; energy is stored in the field.
layers.expert: C=εA/d for parallel plates; U=½CV²; series 1/C=Σ1/Cᵢ; parallel C=ΣCᵢ. Molecular polarisation explains εr; dielectric breakdown limits voltage.

layers.basics: Current is charge flowing per second; resistivity says how much a material opposes it.
layers.deeper: In metals electrons collide with the lattice, giving Ohm’s law; semiconductors have far fewer carriers that can be controlled.
layers.expert: J=σE microscopic Ohm’s law; Drude model σ=nq²τ/m; R=ρL/A; resistivity rises with T in metals, falls in semiconductors.

title: Magnetic fields and forces
summary: Moving charge feels and creates magnetic fields.

layers.basics: Moving charges and currents create magnetic fields and feel forces in them, which is how motors turn.
layers.deeper: Biot–Savart and Ampère’s law give fields of wires and coils; force on a wire is I L × B; Hall effect senses fields.
layers.expert: F=q(E+v×B); ∮B·dl=μ₀I_enc; B of a solenoid μ₀nI; ∇·B=0 (no monopoles).

layers.basics: Changing the magnetic flux through a loop creates an electromotive force; the induced current opposes the change.
layers.deeper: This one law explains generators, transformers, inductors and wireless charging.
layers.expert: ε=−dΦ_B/dt ⇔ ∇×E=−∂B/∂t; motional EMF ε=Blv; eddy currents arise in solid conductors.

title: Inductance
summary: Storing energy in a magnetic field.

layers.basics: A coil resists changes in current because its own changing field induces a counter-voltage.
layers.deeper: Self- and mutual inductance quantify this; energy ½LI² is stored in the field.
layers.expert: v=L di/dt; L=N²μA/ℓ for a solenoid; M=k√(L₁L₂) with coupling 0≤k≤1.

layers.basics: Waves add: peaks meeting peaks reinforce, peaks meeting troughs cancel. Confined waves form standing patterns.
layers.deeper: Transmission lines, antennas, optical cavities and acoustic resonators all rely on the same ideas.
layers.expert: y=A sin(kx−ωt), v=fλ; standing waves with nodes at fixed ends: fₙ=nv/2L; phase velocity vs group velocity.

title: Optics and light
summary: Light as a ray and as a wave.

layers.basics: Light reflects, refracts and diffracts. Lenses and mirrors focus it.
layers.deeper: Snell’s law n₁sinθ₁=n₂sinθ₂ governs fibre guiding; diffraction limits resolution of photolithography.
layers.expert: Rayleigh limit θ=1.22λ/D; thin-film interference; Fresnel equations for reflectance; light is EM waves from ~400 to 700 nm.

layers.basics: Light knocks electrons out of metal only if its frequency is high enough, no matter how bright; this shows light comes in photons.
layers.deeper: Photon energy E=hf; the same physics runs solar cells and photodiodes.
layers.expert: K_max=hf−φ; h=6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s; absorption of a photon with E>E_g creates an electron–hole pair.

title: Quantum mechanics: the basis of semiconductors
summary: Matter behaves as waves with discrete energies.

layers.basics: Electrons confined in atoms or crystals have only certain allowed energies. This explains why materials differ as conductors, insulators and semiconductors.
layers.deeper: Wave functions, the uncertainty principle and tunnelling are the intro to band theory and to why tiny transistors leak.
layers.expert: Time-independent Schrödinger equation −ħ²/2m ψ″+Vψ=Eψ; particle in a box Eₙ=n²π²ħ²/2mL²; Pauli exclusion fills states two electrons at a time.

title: Atomic structure and the periodic table

layers.basics: Atoms have a nucleus and electron shells. Elements in the same column share valence electron counts and so behave alike.
layers.deeper: Silicon (group 14) has four valence electrons, forming a tetrahedral crystal; boron (3) and phosphorus (5) neighbours are the classic dopants.
layers.expert: Electron configuration, ionisation energy and electronegativity trends explain which elements make good conductors, dopants and dielectrics. Si: [Ne]3s²3p².

title: Chemical bonding and material properties
summary: Why materials conduct, insulate or flex.

layers.basics: Metallic bonds leave electrons free to move (conductors); covalent and ionic bonds lock them in place (insulators, semiconductors).
layers.deeper: Silicon’s covalent diamond-cubic lattice gives a small band gap; SiO₂ is a strong insulator, which is why MOS gates and chip isolation work.
layers.expert: Bond strength and bond angles set band gaps and mechanical behaviour; lattice types (diamond, zincblende) matter for III-V devices; thermal conductivity and expansion drive packaging.

layers.basics: A battery turns chemical energy into electricity via oxidation at one electrode and reduction at the other.
layers.deeper: Cell voltage depends on the electrode materials; lithium-ion cells shuttle Li⁺ ions between graphite and an oxide.
layers.expert: Nernst equation E=E°−(RT/nF)ln Q; capacity in Ah, internal resistance and C-rate set practical performance; degradation by SEI growth.
